routes.description: Christian theism is supported cumulatively by a finite cosmic past, fine-tuning, the difficulty of naturalistic abiogenesis, biblical insight, and a redemptive account of suffering.
routes.successCriteria: Show that several substantially independent considerations are more expected under a creator and Christian revelation than under scientific naturalism, while answering the principal scientific and moral objections.

motionBridge.description: The cumulative evidence makes the Christian God more plausible than scientific naturalism does.

centralBridges.description: A finite cosmic past is better explained by a transcendent creator than by matter alone.
Fine-tuning and life's information-rich origin materially favor intelligent design.
Biblical cosmological insight and its theological purpose support Christian revelation.
Suffering is compatible with a redemptive order governed by an eternal-good standard.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Several convergent arguments can support the conclusion without any single absolute proof.
Noncoercive evidence preserves freedom to accept or reject God.

routes.description: Scientific skepticism argues that cosmology and fine-tuning underdetermine God, abiogenesis remains open, Genesis reflects ancient error, and suffering is improbable under Christian benevolence.
routes.successCriteria: Defeat the claimed evidential bridges by exposing unsupported probabilities, viable alternatives, source or textual problems, and unresolved conflict between extensive suffering and a good Christian God.

motionBridge.description: The cited science, biblical claims, and suffering make the Christian God no more plausible and in important respects less plausible.

centralBridges.description: Current cosmology does not establish an absolute beginning or a divine cause.
Fine-tuning does not privilege God over brute fact, necessity, multiverse, or selection accounts.
Genesis contains ancient cosmological features better explained by human authorship.
Prehuman animal suffering and attributed divine violence conflict with Christian benevolence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: An unresolved natural origin of life is not positive evidence of divine design.
Explanatory probabilities require justified distributions and consistent evidential standards.

sections.title: Cosmic beginning and infinity
sections.rationale: The existence of an absolute beginning is a principal claimed scientific implication of theism and receives a direct, technically developed exchange.

proMoves.speaker: Michel-Yves Bollore
proMoves.proposition: The BGV theorem prevents an infinite regress of earlier expanding universes and therefore establishes some absolute cosmic beginning.

sourceSpan.excerpt: They have demonstrated that even if the big bang that we know is not the real beginning... this series is limited and therefore there has been an absolute beginning someday.

proMoves.attributionBasis: The moderator had yielded the dialogue to Bollore, and the sustained first-person defense is followed by Halper's explicit rebuttal.

components.text: The singularity theorems do not establish an absolute beginning.
BGV establishes only a boundary to inflation, not to the universe as a whole.
No observational evidence identifies the proposed absolute boundary.

response.rationale: He directly invokes BGV against an eternal regress, but does not engage the theorem's restricted inflationary scope or provide the observational evidence demanded.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is clear, but the move shifts from past-incomplete expanding models to every possible prior universe and then to an absolute beginning.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A theorem with contested domain conditions is presented as knowledge of an absolute beginning without preserving those conditions.

charity.alternative: BGV may show only that inflationary expansion is past-incomplete while a larger or contracting quantum cosmology remains possible.
charity.decisiveQualification: The theorem's conclusion depends on its average-expansion and classical applicability conditions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from a limited theorem to every possible cosmic history leaves a substantial scope bridge unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A named theorem is relevant evidence, but its conditions and the quoted authors' narrower interpretation are not defended.

responsiveness.rationale: The reply contacts the broad beginning issue but leaves the strongest scope and observational components unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: An absolute beginning materially advances the declared central cosmological bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response treats the skeptical position as requiring an infinite series of expanding big bangs, omitting contracting and quantum alternatives.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 601–628 state the BGV-based finite-series inference; the later exchange develops thermodynamic and infinity claims but does not cure the theorem-scope problem.

conMoves.speaker: Phil Halper
conMoves.proposition: Big-bang and BGV results do not establish that the universe began, because singularity results rely on disputed classical assumptions and BGV bounds inflation rather than the whole cosmos.

sourceSpan.excerpt: The big bang should be understood merely as a theory that says the universe evolved from a hot dense state... The theorem proves that inflation must have a beginning. The universe as a whole, it doesn't.

conMoves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduces Phil's opening statement, and the uninterrupted first-person speech names his book, interviews, and opponent.

response.rationale: This is Halper's opening constructive and precedes every selected pro cosmology move, so it has no earlier selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move consistently distinguishes a hot dense state, a singularity, inflation's beginning, and the universe's beginning.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It concludes that the beginning is unknown rather than impossible and expressly limits what the cited theorems show.

charity.alternative: The theistic case treats singularity and BGV theorems as convergent evidence for an absolute cosmic beginning.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those inferences require classical assumptions and a scope extending beyond inflation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinctions between evidentially supported expansion, singularity assumptions, and global beginning are stable and inferentially connected.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move supplies theorem conditions, named author statements, and a physicist survey, with only bounded verification gaps.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive it clearly anticipates and addresses the central cosmological case presented by the opponent's published position.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the con route's central claim that cosmology does not establish a beginning.

representationalCharity.rationale: It states the theistic theorem-based case in its strong form and then preserves the distinction between our big bang and a deeper beginning.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 19–75 provide the strongest compact statement of the singularity and BGV objections; later dialogue repeats and develops the same proposition.

sections.title: Fine-tuning and competing explanations
sections.rationale: Fine-tuning is a major positive argument, and the debate directly compares design with multiverse, necessity, brute fact, and selection alternatives.

proMoves.speaker: Michel-Yves Bollore
proMoves.proposition: Life-permitting constants are extraordinarily sensitive, have moved scientists toward belief, and are more naturally explained by design because the multiverse lacks direct observation.

sourceSpan.excerpt: If we change just slightly one of these numbers then the universe does not exist... there are billions of other universe and we are lucky... the weakness of that is that nobody has seen anything of multiverse.

proMoves.attributionBasis: Bollore announces that he will explain fine-tuning, uses his cited examples, and Halper immediately answers the claim.

response.rationale: This selected span is the section's positive constructive statement and is not encoded as a reply to an earlier selected move.

precisionFindings.rationale: The design inference is recoverable, but 'fine-tuning,' life-permitting sensitivity, and the relevant range of alternatives remain insufficiently specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Sensitivity and lack of direct multiverse observation do not by themselves establish the asserted comparative probability of design.

charity.alternative: A multiverse could explain observer-compatible constants through selection even if other universes are not directly observed.
charity.decisiveQualification: Indirect theoretical or predictive support can count even without direct observation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The design route is intelligible, but sensitivity is moved to improbability and then to design without a developed probability bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Named scientist examples and constant sensitivity provide relevant material, but no distribution or comparative likelihood is supplied.

responsiveness.rationale: The constructive clearly presents the design case and identifies a perceived weakness in the principal alternative.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the pro route's central design bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The multiverse is reduced largely to unseen multiplicity, omitting its inflationary motivation and claimed predictive uses.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 893–934 contain the strongest compact positive fine-tuning formulation; later repetitions preserve the same sensitivity and design inference.

conMoves.speaker: Phil Halper
conMoves.proposition: Fine-tuning does not privilege God because inflation motivates a multiverse with predictive precedent, while brute fact, necessity, and selection remain live alternatives and no probability distribution has been justified.

sourceSpan.excerpt: It looks better than God... it's implied by inflationary cosmology... Weinberg predicted the value of the cosmological constant using the multiverse... What prediction has God made for anything observable in cosmology?

conMoves.attributionBasis: The exchange explicitly alternates between Bollore and Halper, and this sustained passage is Halper's direct answer to the multiverse objection.

components.text: The multiverse has no relevant evidential support because it is not directly observed.
Design is comparatively favored over the available alternatives.

response.rationale: He answers both decisive components with inflationary motivation and a claimed successful prediction, then explicitly concludes that the multiverse is not evidentially weaker than God.

precisionFindings.rationale: The response clearly distinguishes direct observation from indirect support and frames its conclusion comparatively rather than conclusively.

calibrationFindings.rationale: He expressly says he is not convinced of a multiverse and claims only that it has some evidence and compares favorably with God.

charity.alternative: The design argument cites sensitive life-permitting constants and challenges the empirical standing of an unobserved multiverse.
charity.decisiveQualification: The challenge is comparative and does not require direct observation if an alternative has indirect predictions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The indirect-evidence reply and comparative prediction challenge form a coherent answer to the direct-observation objection.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Inflation and Weinberg's prediction are specific supports, though their exact strength for a multiverse remains compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: The reply contacts both decisive components and states why their failure defeats the asserted comparative design inference.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con fine-tuning bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It acknowledges the opponent's actual evidential concern and even concedes uncertainty about the multiverse before comparing explanations.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 997–1042 are the strongest direct multiverse response; later Q&A adds brute fact, necessity, causal-set selection, and provisional dark-energy qualifications.

sections.title: Origin of life and probabilistic inference
sections.rationale: Abiogenesis is a distinct subsidiary evidential route, contested through the status of current research, expert relevance, and missing probability distributions.

proMoves.speaker: Michel-Yves Bollore
proMoves.proposition: The informational complexity of even a simple cell and the lack of a settled natural pathway make life's origin extraordinarily improbable without fine-tuned design.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Today there is no more idea of how life appeared from inert matter because the density of information... in the DNA of a cell is billion times billion time more dense than in a computer... it's completely improbable.

proMoves.attributionBasis: Bollore explicitly introduces the origin-of-life topic and sustains the first-person argument until Halper's probability question.

response.rationale: This is the selected positive abiogenesis constructive and therefore contains no response targets or components.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is recoverable, but information density, lack of a settled account, impossibility, and improbability are used without stable distinctions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Present scientific uncertainty and biological complexity do not supply the numerical space or sampling assumptions required for the asserted extreme improbability.

charity.alternative: Origin-of-life research has unresolved but active natural hypotheses rather than a completed natural account.
charity.decisiveQualification: Absence of a settled mechanism is not equivalent to evidence that natural origin is nearly impossible.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move shifts from complexity and an unsolved mechanism to extreme improbability without establishing the needed inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The appeal to complexity and unnamed expert discussions is too weak to sustain the quantitative and design conclusions.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive it states a recognizable evidential route, though its warrant is substantially underdeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports a necessary subsidiary component of the cumulative pro case.

representationalCharity.rationale: It portrays current origin-of-life inquiry as having no theory, omitting the live RNA-world and other research programs later named.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 1135–1166 contain the independently necessary abiogenesis burden; the subsequent Wald quotation repeats the same uncertainty-to-improbability inference.

conMoves.speaker: Phil Halper
conMoves.proposition: The abiogenesis inference fails because the cited authority did not research life's origin, active hypotheses exist, and no probability distribution was supplied for declaring a natural origin improbable.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Where do you get the probability distribution... George, he didn't work on origins of life research... many labs around the world [are] working on origins of life. The leading hypothesis... is the RNA world hypothesis.

conMoves.attributionBasis: Halper asks the probability question, challenges the named authority's field, and identifies active research before Bollore interjects.

components.text: Current research supplies no natural account of life's origin.
Cellular complexity establishes that natural abiogenesis is extraordinarily improbable.

response.rationale: The reply identifies active hypotheses and, decisively, the absent probability distribution; it states that these omissions block the claimed improbability inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move separates not knowing the historical pathway from lacking hypotheses and from calculating improbability.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Halper concedes that the origin is unknown while making the narrower claim that the pro probability conclusion is unsupported.

charity.alternative: The pro argument infers design from cellular information, unsettled abiogenesis research, and a Nobel laureate's stated judgment.
charity.decisiveQualification: The authority's expertise and a defined probability model are required for those supports to establish improbability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between an open research problem and a calculated improbability directly exposes the missing inferential bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The disciplinary relevance point and RNA-world example are specific, though the state of the full research field is only summarized.

responsiveness.rationale: Both indispensable components are contacted and the absent-distribution defect is tied explicitly to defeat of the probability conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the con route's subsidiary abiogenesis bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response concedes genuine uncertainty and states the opponent's complexity argument before limiting what follows from it.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 1167–1217 directly challenge the probability model, authority relevance, and claim that no natural hypotheses remain.

sections.title: Genesis and scientific credibility
sections.rationale: Biblical cosmology bears specifically on the Christian identification of God and generates a sustained exchange over alleged insight, ancient parallels, and genre accommodation.

proMoves.speaker: Michel-Yves Bollore
proMoves.proposition: Genesis was scientifically exceptional because the Hebrews rejected celestial divinities and described the sun and moon as created lights despite lacking advanced scientific institutions.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Everybody thought that the sun and the moon were divinity... the only tiny people... thought correctly that the sun and the moon were not divinity but they were just lamp in the sky.

proMoves.attributionBasis: Bollore explicitly begins his Bible case and speaks continuously until Halper's marked rebuttal.

response.rationale: The span is the section's positive biblical constructive, with no earlier selected target encoded.

precisionFindings.rationale: The central comparison is clear, but 'everybody,' 'scientifically right,' and the scope of ancient cultures are unstable or universalized.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A broad uniqueness claim is asserted from selected ancient comparisons without addressing counterexamples or other cosmological claims in Genesis.

charity.alternative: Genesis can be read as an ancient cosmology containing both monotheistic theology and historically common physical conceptions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting celestial gods does not establish scientific accuracy or unique revealed knowledge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move coherently links unusual monotheism to possible revelation, but slides from theological demotion of luminaries to scientific accuracy.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The historical comparison is asserted by reference to the book's survey, while counterexamples and the relevant textual context are not defended.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive it advances a clear biblical evidential route, though it leaves major comparative conditions implicit.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially advances the central revelation bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move depicts virtually all other ancient thinkers as worshiping celestial bodies and does not preserve non-theistic or naturalistic counterexamples.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 1278–1324 are the strongest compact biblical-insight claim; later defenses shift to genre and accommodation rather than adding a separate positive argument.

conMoves.speaker: Phil Halper
conMoves.proposition: Genesis is not scientifically exceptional because its solid firmament reflects widespread ancient cosmology, and selective praise of apparent agreements while excusing errors as non-scientific is inconsistent.

sourceSpan.excerpt: There's nothing special... the sky is a solid dome known as the firmament... the Jewish encyclopedia [and] Hebrew English lexicon... regarded by the Hebrews as solid.

conMoves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly answers Bollore's Bible argument, supplies named textual authorities, and is interrupted by Bollore at the endpoint.

components.text: Hebrew cosmology was uniquely and scientifically correct about the heavens.
That comparative accuracy provides evidence of revelation.

response.rationale: The reply supplies a concrete contrary cosmological feature and named interpretive sources, then states that the claimed scientific uniqueness and revelatory inference fail.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is limited to the firmament and to the inconsistency of using selected scientific concordances as evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The evidence strongly supports an ancient-cosmology reading while the speaker acknowledges interpretive variation rather than claiming every verse is literal.

charity.alternative: Genesis primarily teaches monotheism and may accommodate ancient language rather than functioning as a scientific treatise.
charity.decisiveQualification: That accommodation weakens attempts to count selected apparent scientific agreements as affirmative evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample and anti-selection principle directly undermine the inference from selected agreement to scientific exceptionality.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific textual terminology and multiple named Jewish and Christian interpretive sources support the ancient-firmament claim.

responsiveness.rationale: The reply contacts the uniqueness premise and its evidential consequence and explicitly explains why both are defeated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con biblical-credibility bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It acknowledges metaphorical interpretation and focuses the criticism on inconsistent evidential use rather than requiring crude literalism.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 1437–1475 give the strongest source-backed firmament rebuttal; later discussion adds Enuma Elish parallels and the selective-concordance objection.

sections.title: Animal suffering and divine moral authority
sections.rationale: Prehuman suffering and biblical violence form the principal negative argument against Christian benevolence, with distinct pro defenses based on redemption and divine authority.

proMoves.speaker: Michel-Yves Bollore
proMoves.proposition: Earthly suffering belongs to a post-fall redemptive world in which opportunities for good action enable humanity to return to paradise.

sourceSpan.excerpt: God has sent men to another world... which is what we need today to go back to God... We need to do good deeds and we can do good deeds only in the world where there is unfortunately evil.

proMoves.attributionBasis: Halper explicitly yields after restating the suffering objection, and Bollore gives a sustained first-person theological response.

components.text: Animal suffering predates human sin and therefore cannot result from the human fall.
Evolutionary suffering is difficult to reconcile with a benevolent creator's chosen method.
Biblical commands and actions inflict apparently gratuitous suffering on animals.

response.rationale: The redemptive-purpose account contacts the general purpose of an imperfect world but does not answer the chronology of prehuman suffering or the specific divine-violence examples.

precisionFindings.rationale: The redemptive proposition is clear, but paradise, another world, and the necessity of suffering for good deeds are not sharply delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that good deeds and redemption require an evil world is asserted without comparing less harmful alternatives.

charity.alternative: The objection concerns prehuman animal suffering and specific divine actions, not merely the existence of any hardship permitting moral action.
charity.decisiveQualification: A successful defense must explain the scale, timing, and apparently gratuitous animal suffering.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A soul-making or redemptive route is intelligible, but necessity of this amount and chronology of suffering are left unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The defense relies almost entirely on asserted theology and examples of good deeds without independent support for the world-history claims.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts a central purpose component but leaves the decisive prehuman chronology and specific violence substantially unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central pro suffering bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply initially generalizes the objection into why the world is bad, underrepresenting its prehuman and animal-specific qualifications.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 1850–1899 contain the redemptive-world defense; the immediately following exchange confirms that the prehuman chronology remains unresolved.

proMoves.speaker: Michel-Yves Bollore
proMoves.proposition: Human and animal death is not immoral for God because God can restore life, and eternal separation from God is the only ultimate evil by which divine actions should be judged.

sourceSpan.excerpt: There is only one thing which is bad for God... losing men... for eternity... the only goal of God is to bring as many men back to paradise.

proMoves.attributionBasis: The speaker is directly addressed as Michelle, answers Halper's Amalekite question, and maintains the same first-person theology throughout.

components.text: Biblical commands and actions inflict severe suffering on innocent animals.
Such inflicted suffering conflicts with the claimed benevolence of the Christian God.
The suffering appears unnecessary relative to less harmful divine alternatives.

response.rationale: The move supplies a moral-status distinction between humans and God, but it does not answer why an omnipotent God selected the harmful actions rather than less harmful means.

precisionFindings.rationale: The divine-prerogative thesis is clear, but it moves between death, suffering, restoration, and eternal destiny without specifying whose restoration is guaranteed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion that only eternal separation is real evil is asserted as the controlling standard without a supplied moral argument.

charity.alternative: Even if God may permissibly end life and restore it, deliberately chosen suffering still requires justification when gentler means are available.
charity.decisiveQualification: Authority over life does not by itself answer the necessity or proportionality of inflicted suffering.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The creator-restoration distinction is coherent in outline, but it does not entail that every manner of killing or suffering is morally permissible.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move offers a theological principle but little argument for its exclusivity or application to the specific animal cases.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the moral-authority components but omits the decisive less-harmful-alternative challenge.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly defends the central pro suffering bridge against the biblical-violence objection.

representationalCharity.rationale: It recognizes the actual moral objection but narrows moral evaluation to eternal destiny without engaging the opponent's proportionality concern.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 1956–2051 provide the fullest divine-authority defense and include the infinity exchange that tests its consistency.

conMoves.speaker: Phil Halper
conMoves.proposition: Hundreds of millions of years of prehuman animal suffering and biblical commands or actions harming animals are substantially more expected if the Christian God does not exist than if that God is benevolent.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Animals have been suffering for hundreds of millions of years before humans existed... Why would a good God choose such brutal processes... God ordered the genocide of the Amalekites. He included the animals.

conMoves.attributionBasis: This occurs within Halper's moderator-introduced opening and uses first-person references to his coauthored published argument.

response.rationale: This is the earliest selected suffering constructive, so no earlier selected response target exists.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move identifies distinct temporal, creative-process, command, action, and anthropogenic challenges and gives their comparative conclusion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cumulative evidential direction is supported, though calling nonexistence the simplest explanation compresses possible theodicies and textual interpretations.

charity.alternative: Christianity may explain suffering through human sin, divine purposes, or morally sufficient reasons unavailable to finite observers.
charity.decisiveQualification: The defense must address suffering before humans and suffering directly attributed to divine choices.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The temporal and moral incompatibility arguments are clearly separated and tied to a comparative evidential conclusion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Evolutionary chronology and specific biblical cases are concrete supports, though textual and theological contexts are compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive it directly anticipates the principal fall and greater-good defenses with multiple independently relevant challenges.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central con evil bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately states the human-fall defense before showing why prehuman suffering is a decisive qualification.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 272–320 give the strongest compact five-part animal-suffering case; later dialogue concentrates on the first, third, and fourth challenges.

conMoves.speaker: Phil Halper
conMoves.proposition: A theology that cannot condemn genocide and gratuitous animal killing loses its moral standard, because divine power to restore life does not justify choosing cruel means.

sourceSpan.excerpt: If you can't say because of your religion that a genocide is evil, then you can't say anything isn't evil. You've lost your moral compass... If that isn't evil, what the hell is?

conMoves.attributionBasis: Halper explicitly summarizes Bollore's immediately preceding divine-prerogative answer before the moderator offers Bollore a response.

components.text: God's ability to restore life makes divine killing morally different from human killing.
Only eternal separation from God counts as ultimate evil.
The proposed standard adequately preserves meaningful moral condemnation.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the divine-prerogative standard and explicitly states its defeating consequence: it makes paradigmatic atrocities unavailable as evidence against divine goodness and erodes the moral test.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reductio is clear, though it leaves implicit that restoration might affect the wrongness of death without justifying inflicted suffering.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reductio is powerful against the stated standard, but 'nothing will' rhetorically exceeds what this exchange alone establishes.

charity.alternative: God's unique ability to give and restore life may create moral permissions unavailable to humans.
charity.decisiveQualification: That distinction still needs to justify the chosen suffering and preserve noncircular standards for divine goodness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reductio clearly identifies how insulating every divine act from ordinary moral evidence threatens the asserted benevolence claim.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The critique relies on the opponent's explicit concessions and concrete biblical examples, with a bounded gap concerning restoration.

responsiveness.rationale: All indispensable components of the divine-authority defense are contacted and the defeating moral consequence is expressly stated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly reinforces the central con evil bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately captures the creator-restoration distinction before arguing that it fails to justify cruel means.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 2052–2074 are the decisive moral reductio; Bollore's later response repeats the restoration distinction without addressing proportionality.

pro.rationale: No distinct debate-wide pro consequence survives outside the selected moves, response links, importance judgments, section weights, and route ratings.

eligibility.completionCriterion: The cumulative pro route must comparatively support Christian theism across its scientific, biblical, and suffering bridges.
eligibility.distinctConsequence: No additional consequence remains distinct from the represented route performance.
eligibility.counterfactual: Removing the proposed adjustment would not omit any burden consequence because all identified performance is already represented.

con.rationale: No distinct debate-wide con consequence remains uncaptured by the selected objections, direct replies, importance judgments, weights, and route ratings.

eligibility.completionCriterion: The con route must defeat or materially weaken the principal scientific, biblical, and moral bridges to Christian theism.
eligibility.distinctConsequence: No additional consequence remains distinct from the represented route performance.
eligibility.counterfactual: Removing the proposed adjustment would not omit any burden consequence because all identified performance is already represented.
